claims.claim: Constellium occupies a conversion-and-recycling layer between primary/recycled aluminum supply and aerospace, automotive and packaging demand; its recycling footprint can reduce dependence on energy-intensive primary metal while specialized rolled/extruded alloys retain qualification and manufacturing know-how friction.

The causal advantage is not ownership of an irreplaceable raw-material bottleneck: resilience depends on continued access to primary metal/scrap, energy and qualified downstream demand, while substitution can occur through competing aluminum processors or alternative materials where qualification, weight and economics permit.

A robust 2036 pathway is higher closed-loop scrap use plus high-value aerospace/transport/packaging conversion; the thesis weakens if recycling economics deteriorate, qualified products commoditize, or end-market shortages normalize without operational gains replacing them.

causalEdges: primary/recycled aluminum supply -> Constellium melting/recycling and alloy conversion -> qualified rolled/extruded products -> aerospace/automotive/packaging infrastructure -> mobility, defense and food/beverage needs
higher scrap capture/recycling capacity -> lower primary-metal and energy intensity -> improved input resilience subject to scrap availability and spreads
qualification/manufacturing know-how -> switching friction -> potential pricing/bottleneck value, constrained by competing processors and material substitution

risks.risk: Input resilience remains exposed to primary-aluminum availability, scrap spreads, energy and regional trade conditions.
Automotive rolled-product shortages and favorable scrap dynamics can temporarily amplify economics beyond normalized structural advantage.

unknowns.unknown: Long-run share of economics attributable to durable qualification/process advantages versus cyclical metal and shortage conditions remains uncertain.

claims.claim: Current strength should not be read as pure execution: Q2 adjusted EBITDA contained a large positive non-cash metal-price-lag impact and management has explicitly cited supply shortages and favorable scrap/metal dynamics as contributors.

The strongest falsification test is normalization: if shortages and scrap spreads fade, durable progress should still appear in metal-lag-excluded EBITDA, free cash flow, leverage, recycling utilization and high-value segment economics.

Recycling strengthens resilience but does not eliminate source dependence; Constellium still requires primary metal, scrap, energy and customer qualification cycles, so circularity should be treated as a resilience lever rather than an absolute moat.

risks.risk: Metal-price lag can inflate headline adjusted EBITDA and obscure underlying operating comparability.
Shortage-driven automotive demand and favorable scrap spreads may normalize, testing pricing power and margin durability.
High-value aerospace and automotive exposure carries customer qualification, program-cycle and macro demand dependence; competing aluminum suppliers and alternate materials remain substitutes.

unknowns.unknown: Customer concentration and program-level profitability are not resolved by the reused evidence set.
No independent source in this bounded pass quantifies competitive share durability across major product categories.
